<h2>Biography</h2>
<p>Dr Mesfin Genie is a Senior Lecturer in Health Economics at Newcastle Business School, The University of Newcastle, Australia. His research examines how patients and the public value healthcare, how they process information when making health decisions, and how they respond to health policy. He combines health economics and behavioural economics with discrete choice experiments, eye tracking, health measurement, and decision-support tools.</p>
<p>He received his PhD in Economics from Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Italy, where he used stated-preference methods to study healthcare decision-making. He earned an MSc in Health Economics and Management from the University of Bologna in 2015, an MSc in Economics from Addis Ababa University, and a BA in Economics from Jimma University. He has held research and teaching positions at Ca' Foscari University of Venice, the Health Economics Research Unit at the University of Aberdeen, the Harrison School of Pharmacy at Auburn University, and the School of Medicine at Duke University.</p>
<p>His applied work spans organ transplantation, diabetes, prostate cancer, dementia, loneliness, telemedicine, medical devices, the health workforce, vaccines and vaccine mandates, and broader public-health interventions.</p>

<h2>Research focus</h2>
<div class="editorial-list">
<article class="editorial-row"><p class="editorial-label">01</p><h3>Patient preferences and behavioural economics</h3><p>Discrete choice experiments across health conditions and interventions, with particular interest in preference heterogeneity, equity, and value.</p></article>
<article class="editorial-row"><p class="editorial-label">02</p><h3>Information processing in healthcare decisions</h3><p>Integrating eye-tracking measures with choice experiments to study attention, information acquisition, and multi-attribute choice.</p></article>
<article class="editorial-row"><p class="editorial-label">03</p><h3>Health measurement, outcomes, and policy evaluation</h3><p>Ensuring that policies, technologies, and interventions reflect outcomes that patients and the public actually value.</p></article>
</div>
